analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare insulin costs at $50 a month, ends the Part D coverage gap, and makes drug makers refund wasted vials.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on December 19, 2019, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have redesigned Medicare's prescription drug benefit to eliminate the coverage gap starting in 2022, with brand-name drug makers giving patients a 10% discount at the pharmacy counter after the deductible. It would cap a month's insulin cost at $50 for Part D enrollees after the deductible, make manufacturers refund Medicare for the discarded portion of single-dose vials, tighten payment add-ons for drugs administered in doctors' offices and hospitals, give low-income beneficiaries immediate and retroactive drug coverage, and permanently extend the reduced 7.5% floor on the medical-expense tax deduction. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who spend heavily on prescription drugs, especially people who use insulin, who would pay at most about $50 a month in cost-sharing for insulin after their deductible. Beneficiaries who reach the out-of-pocket threshold get relief from the coverage gap, with manufacturer discounts applied at the pharmacy rather than months later. Low-income people newly eligible for Medicare get immediate drug coverage and, for dual eligibles, reimbursement retroactive up to 36 months. Taxpayers who itemize keep the reduced 7.5% floor for deducting medical expenses, and over-the-counter medicines count as qualified medical expenses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Once a month's insulin costs reach $50 (in 2022, rising with inflation after), the enrollee's cost-sharing for insulin and injection supplies drops to $0, after the annual deductible.

Starting in 2022, the old coverage-gap structure is replaced: manufacturers must give 'applicable beneficiaries' a discounted price equal to 90% of the negotiated price at the point of sale, and the reinsurance share plans pay drops from 80% to 20-30%.

Manufacturers of single-dose or single-use package drugs payable under Part B must refund Medicare quarterly for the amount of the drug that was discarded, subject to a 10% tolerance, with a 25% civil penalty for noncompliance.

Low-income beneficiaries not yet enrolled in a drug plan get immediate point-of-sale coverage, and full-benefit dual eligibles can be reimbursed for drugs bought up to 36 months before enrollment took effect.

The bill slows the growth of the Part D out-of-pocket threshold for 2021-2022 and requires Medicare to pay back beneficiaries who crossed the 2020 threshold and were overcharged under the old formula.

The reduction of the medical-expense deduction floor to 7.5% of income, which was scheduled to lapse after 2020, becomes permanent, and over-the-counter drugs count as qualified medical expenses for health savings accounts.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear new costs: a 10% point-of-sale discount after the deductible, quarterly refunds for discarded single-dose vials, and detailed reporting whenever they raise prices. Hospital outpatient departments and providers take lower Medicare payments for drug administration in off-campus provider departments and a $1,000 cap on add-on payments for expensive Part B drugs. Part D insurers see their reinsurance liability cut sharply, offset by manufacturer discounts.

drawbacks.text: The insulin cap and the manufacturer discounts only apply after the annual deductible, so beneficiaries who never reach the deductible get no benefit from either provision.

The bill never caps or negotiates list prices: it requires manufacturers to report explanations for price increases and disclose discounts, but the discounts owed are percentages of prices the manufacturers themselves set, so underlying drug prices keep rising.
The bill lets each Part D plan sponsor offer up to two additional plans per region (and directs the Secretary to allow more), which can deepen beneficiary confusion in an already crowded market.

The redesigned benefit shifts more cost responsibility onto plans and the government through a new risk-adjustment regime, and the savings depend on manufacturers continuing to honor discount agreements enforced mainly by civil penalties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries this is real, targeted relief — an insulin cap, the end of the donut hole, refunds for wasted drug amounts — paid for largely by manufacturers rather than by patients or general taxpayers. The honest cost side: it takes the softer path on drug pricing. It does not let Medicare negotiate prices or benchmark them to other countries, so list prices keep climbing, and the relief only reaches people past their deductible. Compared with the stronger drug-pricing bills pending in the same Congress, this is a modest package; on its own terms, the benefits to patients outweigh the design limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2019 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID) introduced the bill on December 19, 2019, joined at introduction by five Republican colleagues and eventually 9 Republican cosponsors in total.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; that referral is the last action in the bill's history.
No committee markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the record before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they avoided the point-of-sale discount program, the discarded-drug refunds, and the price-increase reporting the bill would have imposed. Medicare beneficiaries who would have gotten the insulin cap and the end of the coverage gap are worse off, continuing under the older, higher cost-sharing rules.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors — the lead sponsor plus 9 cosponsors — were Republicans, no Democrat cosponsored, and because the bill never reached a vote the record shows no roll-call split either way.

industries.note: The bill makes them pay a 10% discount at the pharmacy after the deductible, refund Medicare for discarded portions of single-dose vials, and report their price increases. It deliberately stops short of price negotiation or international benchmarking, so their power to set list prices survives — the cost falls on their discounts and refunds, not their pricing power.

Drug administration furnished by excepted off-campus provider departments would be paid at the lower physician-office rate, and add-on payments for costly Part B drugs would be capped at $1,000 per drug. The site-of-service change is explicitly excluded from budget-neutrality adjustments, meaning net payment cuts.

Payment for a biosimilar during its initial period would be capped at the reference product's amount, and the Secretary would fund provider education on prescribing biosimilars — both designed to speed biosimilar competition and lower drug prices.

industries.industry: Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The redesigned drug benefit continues to run entirely through private Part D plans, and the bill even lets each sponsor offer up to two more plans per region. Plans lose reinsurance dollars but gain from manufacturer discounts flowing at the point of sale, so the private-plan structure of the benefit is locked in either way.
